title: The Solar Storm That Put Northern Lights Over Cuba
description:
Unreal but true: a new real event every day at 5:48 pm (Riyadh).

On September 1, 1859, astronomer Richard Carrington saw a huge flare on the Sun. About 17 to 18 hours later, the solar storm hit Earth. The northern lights, normally a sight for the far north, were seen as far south as the Caribbean, including Cuba and Hawaii: close to the tropics. Telegraph systems across Europe and North America failed. Some operators got electric shocks, sparks set telegraph paper on fire, and some lines kept working with their batteries disconnected, running on the storm's current alone. It is the strongest geomagnetic storm on record.

The aurora is drawn as a smooth band along one line of latitude on a real map; the real aurora was patchy and its southern edge comes from scattered reports. The counter stops at 23 N, the latitude of Havana and the Tropic of Cancer. It is not in real time.

Sources: NOAA Research, "Independent astronomer records massive solar storm in 1859" (seen as far south as the Caribbean; shocks; sparks set paper ablaze; lines worked without batteries; within 18 hours); Astronomy.com, "Sept. 2, 1859: The Carrington Event peaks" (as far south as the Caribbean and Central America; 17.5 hours); Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Geomagnetic storm of 1859" (as far south as the tropics; ignited recording tape); Physics Today, "Geomagnetic storm" (seen as far south as the Caribbean; telegraphs failed); Wikipedia, "Carrington Event" (Cuba, Hawaii; 17.6 hours); AGU GeoSpace blog, 2018 (seen as far south as Cuba and Hawaii).
Animation drawn in code on a Natural Earth map; narration is AI-generated (ElevenLabs).

Did you guess it? Tell me your number in the comments.
